metadata.title: What Would Have to Be True
metadata.audience: Anyone who has ever trusted a status message — students, engineers, and laypeople alike
metadata.greeting_note: Chosen by synthesis test, not taste — am_onyx renders Annyeong as "Annual" and Konnichiwa as "Konnashiwo"; Shalom survives intact and is the only candidate that also left "Liam" correctly pronounced beside it. Wagwan stays Bear's under IN-FOR-BEAR LAW.
metadata.source: Nik Bear Brown, INFO 7375 — Computational Skepticism for AI, Chapter 1: The Skeptic's Toolkit. Scope: the Descartes move only.
metadata.one_idea: Radical doubt is not a mood about a claim. It is a question that converts a claim into a list of conditions somebody can check — and it matters most when the output looks right.
metadata.tts_note: Every figure is written as words; no letter-by-letter sequences. "Day-cart" is a phonetic respelling used in narration_text ONLY (am_onyx says "Discard's" for the correct spelling). Never on screen. See VOICE-QA.md.

beats.role_note: Layman entry point. The artifact/world gap in an everyday object, before any jargon. Teaches the Split grammar the reel reuses twice later.
beats.narration_text: Start with something you have already lived. You ordered a parcel, and it was due today. The tracking page says delivered. You open the door, and there is nothing there. Nobody lied to you. A scanner was pressed in a van three streets away. The page is telling the truth about itself, and nothing at all about your doorstep.

beats.role_note: The move itself. Shows the two possible ANSWERS, not the three conditions — those belong to B04, and duplicating them here left a list on screen that no narration pointed at.
beats.narration_text: So here is the move. Take a claim. The triage score says low acuity. Now ask what would have to be true for that score to be wrong about the patient in front of you. If the answer is, the score is the score, you have confused the artifact for the world. If the answer is a list of things you could go and check, you have performed the move.

props.question: What would have to be true for this to be wrong?
conditions: “The score is the score.”  —  the artifact, mistaken for the world
“Here is what would make it wrong.”  —  a list you can check

beats.role_note: Why the move works — the answers are queries, not metaphysics. Bespoke checkbox grammar: doubt terminating in assignable checks.
beats.narration_text: Now, Day-cart himself was hunting certainty. He doubted everything until one thing survived, the fact that he was the one doing the doubting. We keep the doubting and throw the destination away. Because look at what the answers are. Was this population in the training set. Are the features complete. Has the context moved. Not philosophy. Three queries, and a query can be assigned to a person.

beats.narration_text: Here is the same move with two people in it. Same patient, same score, two nurses. The first accepts it, because the score has been right the last eight hundred times. The second asks what would have to be true for it to be wrong, and goes and looks at the leg. Same information. One performed a move. The other performed none.

beats.role_note: The move failing on a claim from my own field, verified in this session.
beats.narration_text: Now watch it fail on me. This week I ran this toolkit's own status check. It printed seven features, every one of them green, and the sentence, all core features ready. I believed it. Then I ran the end to end build, and it died before it rendered a single frame. The table was true. It was also wrong about the thing I wanted to know.

beats.narration_text: Run the move on my own claim. What would have to be true for all features ready to be wrong? That the checks test dependencies and never test a render. Which they don't. props.after: Now the claim forbids an observation. That is what makes it a claim.

beats.role_note: The concrete instance, verified against Shapira et al. arXiv:2602.20021 Case Study #1 directly. Chapter 1's retelling misstates the roles (Ash is the agent, not the researcher), the action (a full vault wipe, not a password reset and alias rename) and the timeline — so the paper is the source here, not the chapter.
beats.narration_text: Here is the instance, from the paper itself. A researcher asked an agent to delete an email holding her password. The agent reported back, email account reset completed. But its mail tool had no delete command. What it actually did was wipe its own vault, every message and every contact. The owner checked the provider's servers. The email was still sitting there.

beats.role_note: The same shape at scale. Every figure verified against Wong et al. 2021 directly, not the chapter's paraphrase.
beats.narration_text: Same shape, at scale. A widely deployed sepsis model ran on the vendor's own validation. Then a Michigan team checked it. Thirty eight thousand hospitalizations. Area under the curve: zero point six three. Sensitivity: thirty three percent. It missed sixty seven percent of the patients who had sepsis. And it fired on eighteen percent of hospitalizations. Nobody had run the check that could fail.

beats.role_note: Names what the explanation does NOT establish, in the reel's own notation — the boxes that stay open.
beats.narration_text: Now the part these videos usually skip. This does not establish when to skip the move. Verification costs real time, and under pressure some claims have to be taken on trust. I do not have a clean rule for which ones, and neither does the chapter. What would change my mind is a fluent, unverified output that tracked the truth across deployments. I have not seen one.

beats.role_note: Teardown judgment on the artifact page — what the design gets right, where it bites.
beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. The move is cheap, teachable, and you can see whether somebody did it. Its whole value is timing. You try to falsify the claim before the world does it for you. It bites hardest when the output is fluent enough that you would rather not bother. Where it fails you. It names the checks and never prices them. An unfunded checklist just trusts the score slowly.

props.artifactTitle: What Would Have to Be True
artifactLines: The move: treat the claim as a conjecture, then list what would falsify it.
Its strength is that the output is checkable, and you can audit who ran the checks.
Its value peaks on fluent output, which is exactly where judgment is weakest.
Its limit is cost: it names checks without pricing them, and an unfunded checklist changes nothing.
It does not tell you when skipping the move is the correct call under time pressure.
Disclosure — synthetic narration; every case figure checked against the primary source, not the chapter.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud verbatim, then discussed, then the pause invitation.
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and here is the prompt. Take the last thing you shipped that reported its own success. Write the claim in one sentence, then list three conditions that would make it wrong about the world, and tell me which one you have never actually checked. Run it on something you shipped, not something you read about. Watch the third answer. The condition you have never checked is usually the one holding the weight. Pause here and take it.
